chapters.title: Chapter 1: Two Families of Assets, One Question

lessons.title: Why Alternatives Look Better on Paper Than They Feel in Practice

children.text: Every family WhatsApp group has this story: "Chacha bought a plot near Navi Mumbai for ₹20 lakh in 2011. Today it is worth ₹2 crore." That is ten times the money in 15 years, roughly 16.6% a year, better than the Nifty. Nobody forwards the other stories: the plot in a layout still stuck in litigation, the second flat that sat empty for two years, the startup cheque that went to zero. Alternatives are usually sold to you through their best numbers. This lesson covers the five gaps between the return on the brochure and the return that actually reaches your bank account.

body.text: The return that gets advertised is usually the best-case, pre-cost, survivors-only number. The return you live through is net of every cost, includes the failures, and comes with waiting you cannot skip.

children.text: Gap 1: You Only Hear About the Survivors

markDefs.definition: The distortion that comes from looking only at investments that succeeded or still exist, while failures quietly drop out of the data.

children.text: When a Nifty 50 company collapses, it is removed from the index, but the loss it caused is already baked into the index's history. Alternatives have no such public record. A platform showcases its exited deals. A fund manager raising Fund III talks about the winners from Fund I. A relative remembers the plot that multiplied, not the one that did not. This is
, and it pushes every anecdotal alternative return upward.

body.title: Read the platform's headline
body.question: A fractional ownership platform's homepage says: "Average IRR on exited deals: 17%." It has done 40 deals and exited 9. What is the biggest problem with the headline?
options: IRR is not a real return measure
It covers only the 9 exited deals, which are likely to be the ones that went well
17% is too low to be worth investing for
Platforms are not allowed to publish returns
body.explanation: Deals that go well are the easiest to exit, so exited deals are a flattering sample. The 31 unexited deals may include stalled or underperforming ones. Always ask for returns across every deal the platform has done, realised and unrealised.

children.text: Gap 2: Headline Returns Leave Out the Costs
A Nifty 50 ETF can cost well under 0.1% a year in expenses, and the fund's NAV is already net of them. Alternatives carry far heavier costs, and most of them sit outside the number you are quoted.

body.caption: Costs that sit between the headline return and your bank account
headers: Costs usually missing from the headline

cells: Stamp duty and registration (typically 5 to 8%, varying by state), brokerage, interiors, society maintenance, property tax, repairs, vacancy, capital gains tax
PE, VC or private credit AIF
Management fee, 18% GST on that fee, a share of profits above the hurdle, set-up costs, and idle committed cash
Platform fees, defaults, and tax on interest at your slab rate
Platform and asset management fees, vehicle-level costs, vacancy, and a discount if you exit early
A low expense ratio already reflected in the NAV, plus brokerage and STT when you trade

children.text: Here is what that does to a real-looking property story. A Pune flat is bought in 2014 for ₹50 lakh and sold in 2026 for ₹1 crore. The headline is "doubled in 12 years."

body.caption: n is the number of years held
Pune flat, 2014 to 2026: headline vs after transaction costs (illustrative, price return only)

children.text: Rent helps, but not as much as people assume. Residential rent in Indian cities often yields around 2 to 3% of the property's value before costs, and society maintenance, property tax, repairs and empty months take a real bite out of it. Add back a point or two of net rent and the flat's total return lands roughly in the 6 to 6.5% range before tax, which is bank FD territory, for an asset that took months to sell.

body.title: Calculate a property CAGR
body.prompt: A Kochi flat bought for ₹40 lakh in 2016 is valued at ₹60 lakh in 2026. What is its headline price CAGR over the 10 years, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (₹60 lakh ÷ ₹40 lakh) raised to the power 1/10, minus 1 = 1.5^0.1 − 1 ≈ 4.1% a year. A 50% gain sounds impressive. Spread over a decade, and before any costs, it is below what a bank FD paid over the same period.

children.text: Gap 3: Estimated Value Is Not Money Received

markDefs.definition: A gain that exists only on paper, based on an estimated current value. It becomes realised only when the asset is sold and cash is received.

children.text: Much of the return in a young PE or VC fund, a startup portfolio or a fractional deal is

. A startup's last funding round may value your stake at three times what you paid, but that price was set by a handful of investors for a small new slice of shares, often with special rights you do not have. Until someone buys your shares, the gain is an opinion. In listed markets, the difference between marked value and exit value is usually tiny. In alternatives, it can be the whole story.
Gap 4: Your Money Does Not All Work at Once

When you commit to a PE, VC or private credit AIF, the manager draws your money down over several years. A fund can report an impressive return on the capital it actually invested, while a large part of your commitment sits outside the fund earning much less. You feel the blended result, not the fund's figure.

body.title: Show me the math on idle commitments

children.text: Suppose Neha commits ₹1 crore to a fund. Over the first few years, on average only 60% of her commitment has actually been drawn and invested. The fund reports an 18% return on invested capital. She keeps the undrawn 40% in a liquid fund earning about 6.5%, ready for the next capital call.

content.caption: Neha's blended return on her full ₹1 crore commitment, before fees and tax (illustrative)

children.text: The fund's 18% is real, but Neha's money earned about 13.4%. Chapter 5 explains why IRR on invested capital and your own return on committed money can differ this much.

Some costs never appear in any return figure. RBI tightened its P2P lending rules in August 2024 partly because platforms had marketed loans as investment products with assured returns and quick withdrawal options. Once platforms had to stop offering those features, many lenders discovered that their money could only come back as borrowers repaid. Nothing about the loans had changed. The experience had.

body.title: Headline vs realistic annual returns (%), examples from this chapter

body.text: None of this means alternatives are bad investments. It means their headline numbers and a Nifty index fund's numbers are not the same kind of number. Once you shrink the headline to a realistic figure, you can decide whether the diversification or income is still worth it.

body.title: Arjun's 9.5% office yield
body.scenario: Arjun, an HNI in Hyderabad, is comparing two ways to own office real estate. Option A: listed REIT units on NSE, with a distribution yield of around 6 to 7% and a portfolio of several large office parks. Option B: a ₹25 lakh fractional share of a single pre-leased office floor in HITEC City, advertised at a "9.5% rental yield." The platform charges about 1% of the investment a year in fees.
body.prompt: Estimate what the 9.5% might realistically become, allowing for fees and an average of one vacant month a year. Then list the practical differences that still would not show up in your number.
body.modelAnswer:
Rough net yield:
1. Vacancy: 11 months of rent out of 12 means 9.5% × 11/12 ≈ 8.7%.
2. Fees: 8.7% − 1% ≈ 7.7% a year, before tax.

So the realistic gap over the REIT narrows from about 3 percentage points to roughly 1 point, and the REIT gives daily liquidity on top.

What the number still misses:
- Concentration: one floor and probably one tenant. If that tenant leaves, income drops to zero, not by one month.
- Exit: selling means finding another investor on the platform, possibly at a discount. REIT units sell on NSE the next trading day.
- Valuation: the fractional share is appraised occasionally, while the REIT has a daily market price.
- Platform risk: Arjun depends on the platform's governance and on the vehicle that holds the asset.
- Effort and paperwork: more reporting to read and track, and less standard disclosure than a listed REIT.

body.title: Six questions to ask about any alternative return figure
steps: Is this return gross, or net of all fees, GST, transaction costs and tax?
Does it include every deal or investment, or only the exited and successful ones?
How much of it is cash actually received, and how much is an estimated value?
What period does it cover, and does that period include a bad year like 2020?
Is it the return on money actually invested, or on my full commitment?
What would I realistically receive if I had to exit this month?

cards.definition: Judging returns only from the investments that succeeded or survived, which makes results look better than they were.
Return before fees, taxes and transaction costs are deducted.
A gain based on an estimated value that has not yet been turned into cash through a sale.
Money promised to a fund that the manager has not yet called, which earns only what you earn on it elsewhere.
Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly rate that turns a starting value into an ending value over a given number of years.

points: Alternative returns usually reach you through their best stories, while the failures quietly disappear from view.
Headline figures often leave out stamp duty, brokerage, management fees, GST, vacancy and tax, which can take several percentage points off.
A Pune flat that "doubled in 12 years" compounded at about 5.9% on price, and about 4.7% after purchase and sale costs.
Estimated values and unrealised gains are opinions until someone pays cash for the asset.
In funds that draw money over time, your return on the full commitment is lower than the fund's return on invested capital.
Shrink every headline to a realistic, net, all-deals figure before comparing it with a traditional asset.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or avoid any property, fund, platform or security. All examples and figures are illustrative. Tax and stamp duty rules vary by state and change over time. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before making decisions.
